newsitem.title: UK: LME reforms continue at EGM, more to come.
newsitem.headline: LME reforms continue at EGM, more to come.

text.p: Members of the London Metal Exchange (LME) are believed to have approved changes to the market's constitution at a special meeting on Monday, sanctioning another reform called for by Britain's top regulator last December, metal trade sources said.

At the EGM (Extraordinary General Meeting) held in the LME's board room representatives from the LME's membership of some 100 companies either cast votes in person or by proxy to "open up" the Board by adding two new invited directors.
"Given that this was a SIB (Securities and Investments Board) recommendation and a fairly important one, it was highly unlikely that members would go against it," one source said.
"It would have been like turkeys voting for Christmas," another said.
LME officials were not immediately able to confirm how the voting went, as results will be notified by post to members.

The EGM was called to amend the LME's articles of association, with the Board in future to be comprised of eight directors from ring-dealing companies, three from non-ring dealing firms, and, because of the EGM change, six invited directors.

In a wide-ranging review of the metal market carried out after 1996's Sumitomo Corp scandal the Securities and Investments Board said that the LME Board's composition should better represent the whole membership.

The SIB noted that there had been calls for more directors having no association with the metal industry. Some sources said that the two new invited directors will therefore be a politician and an academic with business knowledge.
However, some metal traders feel that the Board could have been reorganised in a different way.
"I appreciate what the Board is trying to do - I just think there coud have been a better way of doing it," one director at a non-ring dealer said.

As it stands, there remain eight directors representing the 16 category one firms on the floor of the LME. But only two of the three directors who represent non-ring companies are drawn from over 20 category two firms.
Meanwhile, the invited directors, with much less metal industry background, will have to adjudicate on market matters, such as when to intervene and restrict backwardations.
Despite this, the programme of reforms the SIB recommended has further to run, with the LME looking at implementing changes to warehousing, transparency, and information-sharing.
Last week, LME Chief Executive David King said the Exchange will look at ways of reporting large positions as well as ownership of stocks in warehouses, without naming firms.
Restructuring and enlarging the Executive is also on the agenda, he said.

The SIB review was called for by the LME in the wake of Japan's Sumitomo announcing in June 1996 it had lost $2.6 billion in 10 years of unauthorised copper trading carried out by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka - much of it in London.
